summary: A brick tower on a Lake Superior cliff, lit in 1910 after the 1905 storm; both assistant keepers drowned that October. Now a Minnesota Historical Society museum and National Historic Landmark.

access.note: Minnesota Historical Society historic site in Split Rock Lighthouse State Park. As of the October 20, 2026 to January 4, 2027 listing, a grounds pass does not include the lighthouse or keeper's house, which are visited on guided Keeper's Tours on set dates; hours vary by season.

facts.agency: Minnesota Historical Society (site manager); Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (owner, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Act of March 4, 1907 appropriates $75,000 for a light and fog-signal station at or near Split Rock
Construction begins (June 1909 per an Eleventh District paragraph in the clippings file; March 1909 in the station description's cost paragraph); work suspended November 21, 1909

In commission August 1, 1910 per the official report extracts and description, and Pepper (light first shown the night of August 1); July 31 per LighthouseFriends, the MNHS library guide and the MNHS beacon page
Third-order bivalve Fresnel lens per the USLHS archive, LighthouseFriends and the MNHS beacon page; the later station description and Pepper say second-order
Assistant keepers Edward F. Sexton and Roy C. Gill drown in a rowboat on a mail run, October 2, 1910
Concrete tramway completed, replacing the derrick (built 1915-1916)
Light seen at 60 statute miles from a tender on Lake Superior, August 4
Lake Superior highway reaches the station; visitors begin arriving by car
Keepers' families begin to winter at the station year-round
Fog-signal gas engines replaced by diesels
Fog-signal siren converted to a diaphone
Lighthouse Service absorbed by the Coast Guard
Station electrified and a 1,000-watt electric lamp installed (1941 per Pepper)
Coast Guard placed under the Navy; keepers become 'commanding officers'
Fog signal discontinued; last civilian head keeper Robert E. Bennetts retires January 31, 1961
Light decommissioned by January 1, 1969; station declared surplus and given to the GSA
Placed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP 69000073)
Property transferred to the State of Minnesota March 1, 1971
Minnesota Historical Society begins administering the site
Site enlarged from 7.6 to 25 acres; head keeper's dwelling restored
Annual November 10 lighting of the lens for the Edmund Fitzgerald begins (Pepper)
Visitor center opens (greatly expanded 2003 per LighthouseFriends)
Most recent restorations of the lighthouse and fog-signal buildings (2008-2009)
National Historic Landmark

corrections.why: Both the Lighthouse Service's description ('focal plane 168 feet above mean lake level') and the USLHS archive (168 ft) give about 51 m. The record's 40 m (130 ft) is the height of the cliff, not the focal plane.
The record's string looks like a parsing slip. The Service's description says a single white flash every 10 seconds (the lens turns once in 20 seconds with two panels).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station description and a 1911 Eleventh District paragraph in the clippings file say the station went into commission August 1, 1910 (a mid-1910 report extract expected it then), and Pepper says the light was first shown the night of August 1; LighthouseFriends, the MNHS library guide and the MNHS beacon page ('the anniversary of when the beacon was first lit') say July 31, 1910; the 1969 nomination says August 1910. The sources agree on the summer of 1910 and differ by a day.

A mid-1910 report extract says the light was to be 'a third-order light'; the USLHS archive, LighthouseFriends and the MNHS beacon page (third-order bi-valve by Barbier, Bernard et Turenne, Paris) agree; the later station description says second-order with 1,200,000 candlepower and Pepper repeats it; Putnam (1917) lists a 39-inch two-panel lens at 220,000 candles. Not resolved here; third order is the better supported.

notes_for_editor: 1) The 'Split Rock, MN Clippings' file in the USLHS archive is a set of pasted extracts; the clipping does not name volumes or pages, but pen annotations mark the extracts 1908, 1910, 1911 (the Eleventh District paragraph) and 1912 (the station description). The story therefore calls them 'official report extracts' and 'the description' and does not name the Light-House Board or the Service as author. A human should locate the originals (Light-House Board annual reports for 1908, 1909, 1910; Commissioner of Lighthouses report for fiscal 1911) and add page numbers; none of those years is in the local corpus. 2) The Bulletin index entries 'Split Rock light station, received efficiency pennant/flag' (1912-17 p.147, 250; 1918-23 p.218) and keeper 'Wakefield, James' are for Split Rock, New York (Lake Champlain, 3rd district), not Minnesota; the Bulletins' 1915 and 1917 text lists 'Split Rock, N.Y. . . James Wakefield'. They are not used. 3) Disagreements: lens order and candlepower (see resolved_conflicts; the MNHS beacon page says third-order bi-valve, Pepper and the description say second-order); first-lit date (Aug 1 vs Jul 31); electrification 1940 (MNHS timeline, LighthouseFriends) vs 1941 (Pepper); Minnesota Historical Society ownership transfer 1975 (keepers page) vs state 1971 and MNHS administration 1976 (history page and timeline); the MNHS library guide's 'June 30, 1906: Congress approves funding' conflicts with the March 4, 1907 act in the report extract (the story follows the extract); cliff height 124 ft (nomination), 127 ft (description and Pepper), 130 ft (LighthouseFriends and the MNHS lighthouse page); start of construction June 1909 vs March 1909 inside the clippings file; Pepper says the fog signal had diaphones, the description says sirens (diaphone conversion is 1936 per MNHS); 1905 storm toll 36 lives (MNHS, LighthouseFriends) vs over 200 deaths in storms of November 27-29 (Pepper); oil house 1909 (USLHS) vs late 1910 (Pepper) vs built during fiscal 1910 (report extract); distance of the pier 900 ft (description) vs 1,000 ft (Pepper). 4) Roster: LighthouseFriends lists Sterling P. Malone as first assistant 1936-1937 and 1937-1938 with Frank Pohl in between; the USLHS archive has Justus G. Luick to 1936, Frank Pohl 1937, Malone 1937-1938. The USLHS place position (47.3333, -91.6000; 23 km off) is wrong; the station record's position agrees with the NRHP nomination's coordinates. Roster years are the archive's documented spans, not exact terms. Orren P. Young's service at Huron Island is given by Pepper as second assistant from 1901 and first assistant from early 1903 without naming the station for the second post or the station he left in 1908, so no end year is recorded for Huron Island. 5) The 1923 Bulletin note (issue of October 1, 1923, p. 301; Outer Island to Grand Marais, 60 statute miles) is OCR'd badly in the text layer, but the page image reads clearly, including the tender Amaranth; the story says only 'a lighthouse tender' so that every quoted fragment matches the text layer. The 1938 letter (printed p. 104) does not name its writer; the roster has Covell as head keeper then. The 1939 'most visited' article is on printed p. 173 of the 1939 volume. 6) Not found: a contemporary newspaper report of the 1910 drowning or the construction (Chronicling America returned nothing for 'Split Rock' lighthouse 1910-1911; one 1908 hit, a campaign statement by an unnamed congressman in the Ely Miner of August 21, 1908, p. 1, says Split Rock was 'now under construction', which conflicts with the report extracts' June 1909 start and is not used), the Minnesota History article 'The Construction of Split Rock Lighthouse' (vol. 68 no. 5, https://storage.googleapis.com/mnhs-org-support/mn_history_articles/68/v68i05p155.pdf) and the Star Tribune 'Dark day at Split Rock' article were not read and are leads for a human; the NHL nomination (Faltinson 2008) was not available online. 7) The range of 22 is 'visible 22 miles in clear weather' (description) and 'official range of 22 miles' (MNHS); no source states the unit, and the 1923 Bulletin uses statute miles for its observed distances, so range_nm was removed from facts rather than assumed nautical. Tower height 54 ft is LighthouseFriends's and USLHS's figure (base to center of lantern); the 1911 paragraph gives the tower as 38 feet high and the description gives the lantern's focal plane as 38 feet above grade. 8) Pepper's horse and hotel anecdote is repeated as a reported story, not verified. The MNHS hours page lists the Keeper's Tour as 'Saturday (October 23 - November 22)', but October 23, 2026 is a Friday, so the dates look carried over from another year; the story says only that tours are offered on set dates. The 'Today' lens and November 10 statements use the Society's current pages (17, 18, 19); LighthouseFriends's copy is older and undated.
